case_info.scenario: A 13-year-old female was referred to pediatric otolaryngology by the oral surgery clinic for chronic facial pain and abnormal computed tomography (CT) scan findings. Relevant medical history included developmental delay, atrial septal defect, cerebral palsy, and pulmonary artery sling. The patient’s mother reported recurrent sinus infections with associated headaches, facial pain, nasal congestion, facial swelling, and nasal drainage. She had no history of sinus surgery or facial trauma. On physical examination, the patient had an elongated and narrow face, left-sided nasal septal deviation, as well as bilateral enophthalmos. The patient was previously evaluated by oral surgery for multiple impacted teeth; cone-beam CT showed opacified maxillary sinuses and a left-sided molar within the maxillary sinus. Follow-up CT of the sinuses showed bilateral small volume maxillary sinuses with associated opacification, lateralized nasal cavity walls, and inferior bowing of bilateral orbital floors (Figure 1). She subsequently underwent endoscopic sinus surgery. During surgery, bilateral uncinate processes, maxillary ostia, and ethmoid bullae were easily identified. Sinus mucosa was thickened without polyp formation. The retained molar was removed from the left maxillary sinus endoscopically.

case_info.explanation: A. Bilateral silent sinus syndrome Silent sinus syndrome (SSS) is a condition of maxillary sinus wall collapse with resulting enophthalmos from orbital floor collapse.1The cause is believed to be an obstructive process of the natural maxillary sinus ostium that induces a negative pressure within the sinus leading to collapse of all maxillary sinus walls.2Patients with SSS generally lack a significant history of infection, trauma, congenital anomaly, or sinus surgery. The literature suggests, however, that most patients can present with associated acute or chronic sinonasal symptoms.3Additionally, SSS can present with facial asymmetry and multiple ophthalmologic complications including enophthalmos, hypoglobus, and diplopia. The systematic literature review by Rosso et al2revealed the most common and consistent diagnostic criteria for SSS is the presence of enophthalmos and maxillary atelectasis, which is defined as persistent reduction in maxillary sinus volume due to inward bowing of antral walls. The criterion standard treatment for SSS involves reestablishing the integrity of the maxillary sinus via functional endoscopic sinus surgery with possible orbital floor reconstruction when indicated.2Unilateral SSS is rare in and of itself, but the presence of SSS bilaterally has only been documented a handful of times in the literature. Additionally, documentation of SSS in the pediatric population is uncommon.4The presence of bilateral enophthalmos due to SSS is extremely rare but nonetheless plausible in this case. While both SSS and maxillary sinus hypoplasia involve the maxillary sinus, they represent different clinical entities. Maxillary sinus aplasia and hypoplasia involve a congenital or developmental absence or reduction in the size of the maxillary sinus, whereas in SSS, the sinus was initially normal, but later collapsed. The maxillary sinuses normally develop beginning in the third gestational month and progress through the individual’s eighth year of life. Sinonasal complications can present following interruption or arrest of normal development. The incidence of maxillary sinus hypoplasia ranges between 1.5% and 10% and can present asymptomatically or with associated facial pain and pressure, headaches, nasal congestion, nasal drainage, and voice changes. Additionally, maxillary sinus hypoplasia is typically associated with hypoplastic or absent uncinate process.5CT imaging is the criterion standard for identifying this pathology and distinguishing it from similar conditions.6Key distinguishing radiographic findings in maxillary sinus hypoplasia include a small, underdeveloped sinus with intact orbital floor and nasal wall. In SSS, a degree of collapse of all maxillary sinus walls would be expected. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder associated with the production of thick mucosal secretions that can obstruct airways and cause an array of respiratory symptoms. It is caused by variants in theCFTRgene. CF with sinonasal polyposis is a condition that presents with benign growths (polyps) in the nasal passages. These can obstruct the airway and exacerbate respiratory symptoms leading to recurrent sinus infections and increased trouble with breathing. Additionally, these can present with persistent nasal congestion and drainage, facial pain and pressure, and alterations in sense of smell. In contrast to SSS, patients with CF can present with evidence of widespread sinus changes, obstruction, and opacification due to polyposis and mucus plugging. Additionally, inferior displacement of the orbital floor would be unexpected. It has been reported that chronic infection and inflammation resulting from complications from CF can alter the growth and development of sinuses, leading to hypoplasia.7 A 2020 publication by Albadr et al8noted that diagnosis of SSS relies on a review of imaging that reveals reduction in size of the maxillary sinus antrum and inward bowing of most or all maxillary sinus walls. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. This can also be seen endoscopically (Figure 2).

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Bilateral silent sinus syndrome Silent sinus syndrome (SSS) is a condition of maxillary sinus wall collapse with resulting enophthalmos from orbital floor collapse.1The cause is believed to be an obstructive process of the natural maxillary sinus ostium that induces a negative pressure within the sinus leading to collapse of all maxillary sinus walls.2Patients with SSS generally lack a significant history of infection, trauma, congenital anomaly, or sinus surgery. The literature suggests, however, that most patients can present with associated acute or chronic sinonasal symptoms.3Additionally, SSS can present with facial asymmetry and multiple ophthalmologic complications including enophthalmos, hypoglobus, and diplopia. The systematic literature review by Rosso et al2revealed the most common and consistent diagnostic criteria for SSS is the presence of enophthalmos and maxillary atelectasis, which is defined as persistent reduction in maxillary sinus volume due to inward bowing of antral walls. The criterion standard treatment for SSS involves reestablishing the integrity of the maxillary sinus via functional endoscopic sinus surgery with possible orbital floor reconstruction when indicated.2Unilateral SSS is rare in and of itself, but the presence of SSS bilaterally has only been documented a handful of times in the literature. Additionally, documentation of SSS in the pediatric population is uncommon.4The presence of bilateral enophthalmos due to SSS is extremely rare but nonetheless plausible in this case. While both SSS and maxillary sinus hypoplasia involve the maxillary sinus, they represent different clinical entities. Maxillary sinus aplasia and hypoplasia involve a congenital or developmental absence or reduction in the size of the maxillary sinus, whereas in SSS, the sinus was initially normal, but later collapsed. The maxillary sinuses normally develop beginning in the third gestational month and progress through the individual’s eighth year of life. Sinonasal complications can present following interruption or arrest of normal development. The incidence of maxillary sinus hypoplasia ranges between 1.5% and 10% and can present asymptomatically or with associated facial pain and pressure, headaches, nasal congestion, nasal drainage, and voice changes. Additionally, maxillary sinus hypoplasia is typically associated with hypoplastic or absent uncinate process.5CT imaging is the criterion standard for identifying this pathology and distinguishing it from similar conditions.6Key distinguishing radiographic findings in maxillary sinus hypoplasia include a small, underdeveloped sinus with intact orbital floor and nasal wall. In SSS, a degree of collapse of all maxillary sinus walls would be expected. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder associated with the production of thick mucosal secretions that can obstruct airways and cause an array of respiratory symptoms. It is caused by variants in theCFTRgene. CF with sinonasal polyposis is a condition that presents with benign growths (polyps) in the nasal passages. These can obstruct the airway and exacerbate respiratory symptoms leading to recurrent sinus infections and increased trouble with breathing. Additionally, these can present with persistent nasal congestion and drainage, facial pain and pressure, and alterations in sense of smell. In contrast to SSS, patients with CF can present with evidence of widespread sinus changes, obstruction, and opacification due to polyposis and mucus plugging. Additionally, inferior displacement of the orbital floor would be unexpected. It has been reported that chronic infection and inflammation resulting from complications from CF can alter the growth and development of sinuses, leading to hypoplasia.7 A 2020 publication by Albadr et al8noted that diagnosis of SSS relies on a review of imaging that reveals reduction in size of the maxillary sinus antrum and inward bowing of most or all maxillary sinus walls. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. This can also be seen endoscopically (Figure 2).

case_info.explanation: A. Bilateral silent sinus syndrome Silent sinus syndrome (SSS) is a condition of maxillary sinus wall collapse with resulting enophthalmos from orbital floor collapse.1The cause is believed to be an obstructive process of the natural maxillary sinus ostium that induces a negative pressure within the sinus leading to collapse of all maxillary sinus walls.2Patients with SSS generally lack a significant history of infection, trauma, congenital anomaly, or sinus surgery. The literature suggests, however, that most patients can present with associated acute or chronic sinonasal symptoms.3Additionally, SSS can present with facial asymmetry and multiple ophthalmologic complications including enophthalmos, hypoglobus, and diplopia. The systematic literature review by Rosso et al2revealed the most common and consistent diagnostic criteria for SSS is the presence of enophthalmos and maxillary atelectasis, which is defined as persistent reduction in maxillary sinus volume due to inward bowing of antral walls. The criterion standard treatment for SSS involves reestablishing the integrity of the maxillary sinus via functional endoscopic sinus surgery with possible orbital floor reconstruction when indicated.2Unilateral SSS is rare in and of itself, but the presence of SSS bilaterally has only been documented a handful of times in the literature. Additionally, documentation of SSS in the pediatric population is uncommon.4The presence of bilateral enophthalmos due to SSS is extremely rare but nonetheless plausible in this case. While both SSS and maxillary sinus hypoplasia involve the maxillary sinus, they represent different clinical entities. Maxillary sinus aplasia and hypoplasia involve a congenital or developmental absence or reduction in the size of the maxillary sinus, whereas in SSS, the sinus was initially normal, but later collapsed. The maxillary sinuses normally develop beginning in the third gestational month and progress through the individual’s eighth year of life. Sinonasal complications can present following interruption or arrest of normal development. The incidence of maxillary sinus hypoplasia ranges between 1.5% and 10% and can present asymptomatically or with associated facial pain and pressure, headaches, nasal congestion, nasal drainage, and voice changes. Additionally, maxillary sinus hypoplasia is typically associated with hypoplastic or absent uncinate process.5CT imaging is the criterion standard for identifying this pathology and distinguishing it from similar conditions.6Key distinguishing radiographic findings in maxillary sinus hypoplasia include a small, underdeveloped sinus with intact orbital floor and nasal wall. In SSS, a degree of collapse of all maxillary sinus walls would be expected. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder associated with the production of thick mucosal secretions that can obstruct airways and cause an array of respiratory symptoms. It is caused by variants in theCFTRgene. CF with sinonasal polyposis is a condition that presents with benign growths (polyps) in the nasal passages. These can obstruct the airway and exacerbate respiratory symptoms leading to recurrent sinus infections and increased trouble with breathing. Additionally, these can present with persistent nasal congestion and drainage, facial pain and pressure, and alterations in sense of smell. In contrast to SSS, patients with CF can present with evidence of widespread sinus changes, obstruction, and opacification due to polyposis and mucus plugging. Additionally, inferior displacement of the orbital floor would be unexpected. It has been reported that chronic infection and inflammation resulting from complications from CF can alter the growth and development of sinuses, leading to hypoplasia.7 A 2020 publication by Albadr et al8noted that diagnosis of SSS relies on a review of imaging that reveals reduction in size of the maxillary sinus antrum and inward bowing of most or all maxillary sinus walls. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. This can also be seen endoscopically (Figure 2).

case_info.explanation: A. Bilateral silent sinus syndrome Silent sinus syndrome (SSS) is a condition of maxillary sinus wall collapse with resulting enophthalmos from orbital floor collapse.1The cause is believed to be an obstructive process of the natural maxillary sinus ostium that induces a negative pressure within the sinus leading to collapse of all maxillary sinus walls.2Patients with SSS generally lack a significant history of infection, trauma, congenital anomaly, or sinus surgery. The literature suggests, however, that most patients can present with associated acute or chronic sinonasal symptoms.3Additionally, SSS can present with facial asymmetry and multiple ophthalmologic complications including enophthalmos, hypoglobus, and diplopia. The systematic literature review by Rosso et al2revealed the most common and consistent diagnostic criteria for SSS is the presence of enophthalmos and maxillary atelectasis, which is defined as persistent reduction in maxillary sinus volume due to inward bowing of antral walls. The criterion standard treatment for SSS involves reestablishing the integrity of the maxillary sinus via functional endoscopic sinus surgery with possible orbital floor reconstruction when indicated.2Unilateral SSS is rare in and of itself, but the presence of SSS bilaterally has only been documented a handful of times in the literature. Additionally, documentation of SSS in the pediatric population is uncommon.4The presence of bilateral enophthalmos due to SSS is extremely rare but nonetheless plausible in this case. While both SSS and maxillary sinus hypoplasia involve the maxillary sinus, they represent different clinical entities. Maxillary sinus aplasia and hypoplasia involve a congenital or developmental absence or reduction in the size of the maxillary sinus, whereas in SSS, the sinus was initially normal, but later collapsed. The maxillary sinuses normally develop beginning in the third gestational month and progress through the individual’s eighth year of life. Sinonasal complications can present following interruption or arrest of normal development. The incidence of maxillary sinus hypoplasia ranges between 1.5% and 10% and can present asymptomatically or with associated facial pain and pressure, headaches, nasal congestion, nasal drainage, and voice changes. Additionally, maxillary sinus hypoplasia is typically associated with hypoplastic or absent uncinate process.5CT imaging is the criterion standard for identifying this pathology and distinguishing it from similar conditions.6Key distinguishing radiographic findings in maxillary sinus hypoplasia include a small, underdeveloped sinus with intact orbital floor and nasal wall. In SSS, a degree of collapse of all maxillary sinus walls would be expected. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder associated with the production of thick mucosal secretions that can obstruct airways and cause an array of respiratory symptoms. It is caused by variants in theCFTRgene. CF with sinonasal polyposis is a condition that presents with benign growths (polyps) in the nasal passages. These can obstruct the airway and exacerbate respiratory symptoms leading to recurrent sinus infections and increased trouble with breathing. Additionally, these can present with persistent nasal congestion and drainage, facial pain and pressure, and alterations in sense of smell. In contrast to SSS, patients with CF can present with evidence of widespread sinus changes, obstruction, and opacification due to polyposis and mucus plugging. Additionally, inferior displacement of the orbital floor would be unexpected. It has been reported that chronic infection and inflammation resulting from complications from CF can alter the growth and development of sinuses, leading to hypoplasia.7 A 2020 publication by Albadr et al8noted that diagnosis of SSS relies on a review of imaging that reveals reduction in size of the maxillary sinus antrum and inward bowing of most or all maxillary sinus walls. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. This can also be seen endoscopically (Figure 2).

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: A. Bilateral silent sinus syndrome Silent sinus syndrome (SSS) is a condition of maxillary sinus wall collapse with resulting enophthalmos from orbital floor collapse.1The cause is believed to be an obstructive process of the natural maxillary sinus ostium that induces a negative pressure within the sinus leading to collapse of all maxillary sinus walls.2Patients with SSS generally lack a significant history of infection, trauma, congenital anomaly, or sinus surgery. The literature suggests, however, that most patients can present with associated acute or chronic sinonasal symptoms.3Additionally, SSS can present with facial asymmetry and multiple ophthalmologic complications including enophthalmos, hypoglobus, and diplopia. The systematic literature review by Rosso et al2revealed the most common and consistent diagnostic criteria for SSS is the presence of enophthalmos and maxillary atelectasis, which is defined as persistent reduction in maxillary sinus volume due to inward bowing of antral walls. The criterion standard treatment for SSS involves reestablishing the integrity of the maxillary sinus via functional endoscopic sinus surgery with possible orbital floor reconstruction when indicated.2Unilateral SSS is rare in and of itself, but the presence of SSS bilaterally has only been documented a handful of times in the literature. Additionally, documentation of SSS in the pediatric population is uncommon.4The presence of bilateral enophthalmos due to SSS is extremely rare but nonetheless plausible in this case. While both SSS and maxillary sinus hypoplasia involve the maxillary sinus, they represent different clinical entities. Maxillary sinus aplasia and hypoplasia involve a congenital or developmental absence or reduction in the size of the maxillary sinus, whereas in SSS, the sinus was initially normal, but later collapsed. The maxillary sinuses normally develop beginning in the third gestational month and progress through the individual’s eighth year of life. Sinonasal complications can present following interruption or arrest of normal development. The incidence of maxillary sinus hypoplasia ranges between 1.5% and 10% and can present asymptomatically or with associated facial pain and pressure, headaches, nasal congestion, nasal drainage, and voice changes. Additionally, maxillary sinus hypoplasia is typically associated with hypoplastic or absent uncinate process.5CT imaging is the criterion standard for identifying this pathology and distinguishing it from similar conditions.6Key distinguishing radiographic findings in maxillary sinus hypoplasia include a small, underdeveloped sinus with intact orbital floor and nasal wall. In SSS, a degree of collapse of all maxillary sinus walls would be expected. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder associated with the production of thick mucosal secretions that can obstruct airways and cause an array of respiratory symptoms. It is caused by variants in theCFTRgene. CF with sinonasal polyposis is a condition that presents with benign growths (polyps) in the nasal passages. These can obstruct the airway and exacerbate respiratory symptoms leading to recurrent sinus infections and increased trouble with breathing. Additionally, these can present with persistent nasal congestion and drainage, facial pain and pressure, and alterations in sense of smell. In contrast to SSS, patients with CF can present with evidence of widespread sinus changes, obstruction, and opacification due to polyposis and mucus plugging. Additionally, inferior displacement of the orbital floor would be unexpected. It has been reported that chronic infection and inflammation resulting from complications from CF can alter the growth and development of sinuses, leading to hypoplasia.7 A 2020 publication by Albadr et al8noted that diagnosis of SSS relies on a review of imaging that reveals reduction in size of the maxillary sinus antrum and inward bowing of most or all maxillary sinus walls. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. This can also be seen endoscopically (Figure 2).

     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

case_info.explanation: A. Bilateral silent sinus syndrome Silent sinus syndrome (SSS) is a condition of maxillary sinus wall collapse with resulting enophthalmos from orbital floor collapse.1The cause is believed to be an obstructive process of the natural maxillary sinus ostium that induces a negative pressure within the sinus leading to collapse of all maxillary sinus walls.2Patients with SSS generally lack a significant history of infection, trauma, congenital anomaly, or sinus surgery. The literature suggests, however, that most patients can present with associated acute or chronic sinonasal symptoms.3Additionally, SSS can present with facial asymmetry and multiple ophthalmologic complications including enophthalmos, hypoglobus, and diplopia. The systematic literature review by Rosso et al2revealed the most common and consistent diagnostic criteria for SSS is the presence of enophthalmos and maxillary atelectasis, which is defined as persistent reduction in maxillary sinus volume due to inward bowing of antral walls. The criterion standard treatment for SSS involves reestablishing the integrity of the maxillary sinus via functional endoscopic sinus surgery with possible orbital floor reconstruction when indicated.2Unilateral SSS is rare in and of itself, but the presence of SSS bilaterally has only been documented a handful of times in the literature. Additionally, documentation of SSS in the pediatric population is uncommon.4The presence of bilateral enophthalmos due to SSS is extremely rare but nonetheless plausible in this case. While both SSS and maxillary sinus hypoplasia involve the maxillary sinus, they represent different clinical entities. Maxillary sinus aplasia and hypoplasia involve a congenital or developmental absence or reduction in the size of the maxillary sinus, whereas in SSS, the sinus was initially normal, but later collapsed. The maxillary sinuses normally develop beginning in the third gestational month and progress through the individual’s eighth year of life. Sinonasal complications can present following interruption or arrest of normal development. The incidence of maxillary sinus hypoplasia ranges between 1.5% and 10% and can present asymptomatically or with associated facial pain and pressure, headaches, nasal congestion, nasal drainage, and voice changes. Additionally, maxillary sinus hypoplasia is typically associated with hypoplastic or absent uncinate process.5CT imaging is the criterion standard for identifying this pathology and distinguishing it from similar conditions.6Key distinguishing radiographic findings in maxillary sinus hypoplasia include a small, underdeveloped sinus with intact orbital floor and nasal wall. In SSS, a degree of collapse of all maxillary sinus walls would be expected. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder associated with the production of thick mucosal secretions that can obstruct airways and cause an array of respiratory symptoms. It is caused by variants in theCFTRgene. CF with sinonasal polyposis is a condition that presents with benign growths (polyps) in the nasal passages. These can obstruct the airway and exacerbate respiratory symptoms leading to recurrent sinus infections and increased trouble with breathing. Additionally, these can present with persistent nasal congestion and drainage, facial pain and pressure, and alterations in sense of smell. In contrast to SSS, patients with CF can present with evidence of widespread sinus changes, obstruction, and opacification due to polyposis and mucus plugging. Additionally, inferior displacement of the orbital floor would be unexpected. It has been reported that chronic infection and inflammation resulting from complications from CF can alter the growth and development of sinuses, leading to hypoplasia.7 A 2020 publication by Albadr et al8noted that diagnosis of SSS relies on a review of imaging that reveals reduction in size of the maxillary sinus antrum and inward bowing of most or all maxillary sinus walls. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. This can also be seen endoscopically (Figure 2).

case_info.explanation: A. Bilateral silent sinus syndrome Silent sinus syndrome (SSS) is a condition of maxillary sinus wall collapse with resulting enophthalmos from orbital floor collapse.1The cause is believed to be an obstructive process of the natural maxillary sinus ostium that induces a negative pressure within the sinus leading to collapse of all maxillary sinus walls.2Patients with SSS generally lack a significant history of infection, trauma, congenital anomaly, or sinus surgery. The literature suggests, however, that most patients can present with associated acute or chronic sinonasal symptoms.3Additionally, SSS can present with facial asymmetry and multiple ophthalmologic complications including enophthalmos, hypoglobus, and diplopia. The systematic literature review by Rosso et al2revealed the most common and consistent diagnostic criteria for SSS is the presence of enophthalmos and maxillary atelectasis, which is defined as persistent reduction in maxillary sinus volume due to inward bowing of antral walls. The criterion standard treatment for SSS involves reestablishing the integrity of the maxillary sinus via functional endoscopic sinus surgery with possible orbital floor reconstruction when indicated.2Unilateral SSS is rare in and of itself, but the presence of SSS bilaterally has only been documented a handful of times in the literature. Additionally, documentation of SSS in the pediatric population is uncommon.4The presence of bilateral enophthalmos due to SSS is extremely rare but nonetheless plausible in this case. While both SSS and maxillary sinus hypoplasia involve the maxillary sinus, they represent different clinical entities. Maxillary sinus aplasia and hypoplasia involve a congenital or developmental absence or reduction in the size of the maxillary sinus, whereas in SSS, the sinus was initially normal, but later collapsed. The maxillary sinuses normally develop beginning in the third gestational month and progress through the individual’s eighth year of life. Sinonasal complications can present following interruption or arrest of normal development. The incidence of maxillary sinus hypoplasia ranges between 1.5% and 10% and can present asymptomatically or with associated facial pain and pressure, headaches, nasal congestion, nasal drainage, and voice changes. Additionally, maxillary sinus hypoplasia is typically associated with hypoplastic or absent uncinate process.5CT imaging is the criterion standard for identifying this pathology and distinguishing it from similar conditions.6Key distinguishing radiographic findings in maxillary sinus hypoplasia include a small, underdeveloped sinus with intact orbital floor and nasal wall. In SSS, a degree of collapse of all maxillary sinus walls would be expected. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder associated with the production of thick mucosal secretions that can obstruct airways and cause an array of respiratory symptoms. It is caused by variants in theCFTRgene. CF with sinonasal polyposis is a condition that presents with benign growths (polyps) in the nasal passages. These can obstruct the airway and exacerbate respiratory symptoms leading to recurrent sinus infections and increased trouble with breathing. Additionally, these can present with persistent nasal congestion and drainage, facial pain and pressure, and alterations in sense of smell. In contrast to SSS, patients with CF can present with evidence of widespread sinus changes, obstruction, and opacification due to polyposis and mucus plugging. Additionally, inferior displacement of the orbital floor would be unexpected. It has been reported that chronic infection and inflammation resulting from complications from CF can alter the growth and development of sinuses, leading to hypoplasia.7 A 2020 publication by Albadr et al8noted that diagnosis of SSS relies on a review of imaging that reveals reduction in size of the maxillary sinus antrum and inward bowing of most or all maxillary sinus walls. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. This can also be seen endoscopically (Figure 2).

The patient was previously evaluated by oral surgery for multiple impacted teeth; cone-beam CT showed opacified maxillary sinuses and a left-sided molar within the maxillary sinus. Follow-up CT of the sinuses showed bilateral small volume maxillary sinuses with associated opacification, lateralized nasal cavity walls, and inferior bowing of bilateral orbital floors (Figure 1). She subsequently underwent endoscopic sinus surgery. During surgery, bilateral uncinate processes, maxillary ostia, and ethmoid bullae were easily identified. Sinus mucosa was thickened without polyp formation. The retained molar was removed from the left maxillary sinus endoscopically.

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Bilateral silent sinus syndrome Silent sinus syndrome (SSS) is a condition of maxillary sinus wall collapse with resulting enophthalmos from orbital floor collapse.1The cause is believed to be an obstructive process of the natural maxillary sinus ostium that induces a negative pressure within the sinus leading to collapse of all maxillary sinus walls.2Patients with SSS generally lack a significant history of infection, trauma, congenital anomaly, or sinus surgery. The literature suggests, however, that most patients can present with associated acute or chronic sinonasal symptoms.3Additionally, SSS can present with facial asymmetry and multiple ophthalmologic complications including enophthalmos, hypoglobus, and diplopia. The systematic literature review by Rosso et al2revealed the most common and consistent diagnostic criteria for SSS is the presence of enophthalmos and maxillary atelectasis, which is defined as persistent reduction in maxillary sinus volume due to inward bowing of antral walls. The criterion standard treatment for SSS involves reestablishing the integrity of the maxillary sinus via functional endoscopic sinus surgery with possible orbital floor reconstruction when indicated.2Unilateral SSS is rare in and of itself, but the presence of SSS bilaterally has only been documented a handful of times in the literature. Additionally, documentation of SSS in the pediatric population is uncommon.4The presence of bilateral enophthalmos due to SSS is extremely rare but nonetheless plausible in this case. While both SSS and maxillary sinus hypoplasia involve the maxillary sinus, they represent different clinical entities. Maxillary sinus aplasia and hypoplasia involve a congenital or developmental absence or reduction in the size of the maxillary sinus, whereas in SSS, the sinus was initially normal, but later collapsed. The maxillary sinuses normally develop beginning in the third gestational month and progress through the individual’s eighth year of life. Sinonasal complications can present following interruption or arrest of normal development. The incidence of maxillary sinus hypoplasia ranges between 1.5% and 10% and can present asymptomatically or with associated facial pain and pressure, headaches, nasal congestion, nasal drainage, and voice changes. Additionally, maxillary sinus hypoplasia is typically associated with hypoplastic or absent uncinate process.5CT imaging is the criterion standard for identifying this pathology and distinguishing it from similar conditions.6Key distinguishing radiographic findings in maxillary sinus hypoplasia include a small, underdeveloped sinus with intact orbital floor and nasal wall. In SSS, a degree of collapse of all maxillary sinus walls would be expected. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder associated with the production of thick mucosal secretions that can obstruct airways and cause an array of respiratory symptoms. It is caused by variants in theCFTRgene. CF with sinonasal polyposis is a condition that presents with benign growths (polyps) in the nasal passages. These can obstruct the airway and exacerbate respiratory symptoms leading to recurrent sinus infections and increased trouble with breathing. Additionally, these can present with persistent nasal congestion and drainage, facial pain and pressure, and alterations in sense of smell. In contrast to SSS, patients with CF can present with evidence of widespread sinus changes, obstruction, and opacification due to polyposis and mucus plugging. Additionally, inferior displacement of the orbital floor would be unexpected. It has been reported that chronic infection and inflammation resulting from complications from CF can alter the growth and development of sinuses, leading to hypoplasia.7 A 2020 publication by Albadr et al8noted that diagnosis of SSS relies on a review of imaging that reveals reduction in size of the maxillary sinus antrum and inward bowing of most or all maxillary sinus walls. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. Additionally, the presence of a large middle meatus and laterally deviated uncinate is included among the most common findings in patients with SSS. This can also be seen endoscopically (Figure 2).
